subject: ela
description: Students demonstrate understanding of figurative language, word relationships, and nuances in word meanings. They interpret figures of speech in context, especially personification, and explain their meaning. They use the relationship between particular words (for example cause/effect, part/whole, item/category) to better understand each of the words. They distinguish among the connotations (associations) of words with similar denotations (definitions), such as stingy, scrimping, economical, unwasteful, and thrifty. Every item embeds the full sentence, line, or short passage it depends on, so the student needs nothing external.
subSkills: Interpret figures of speech in context, including personification, simile, metaphor, hyperbole, and idiom, and explain what each figure means
Use the relationship between particular words to better understand each word: cause/effect, part/whole, item/category, synonym, and antonym
Complete and interpret word analogies that express a relationship (for example part/whole or item/category)
Distinguish among the connotations of words with similar denotations and place words on a scale from positive to neutral to negative
Choose the word whose nuance or connotation best fits the tone and meaning of a sentence

problemArchetypes.name: Interpret a figure of speech in context
problemArchetypes.example: Read the line: 'The old floorboards groaned and complained every time we tiptoed down the hall.' What does this personification suggest about the floorboards? Answer: The floorboards make loud creaking noises, so the writer describes them as if they are tired, unhappy people who object to being walked on.

problemArchetypes.name: Identify the type of figurative language
problemArchetypes.example: Read the sentence: 'My backpack weighed a thousand pounds by the end of the school day.' Which figure of speech is used? Answer: Hyperbole, because the writer exaggerates the weight to show how heavy and tiring the backpack felt.

problemArchetypes.name: Use a word relationship to understand a word
problemArchetypes.example: Consider the pair 'petal' and 'flower.' What relationship connects them, and how does it help you understand 'petal'? Answer: Part to whole; a petal is one part of a flower, so knowing the whole flower helps you picture where the petal belongs.

problemArchetypes.name: Complete a word analogy
problemArchetypes.example: Finish the analogy: 'finger is to hand as branch is to ____.' Answer: tree, because a finger is a part of a hand just as a branch is a part of a tree (part to whole).

problemArchetypes.name: Distinguish connotations of near-synonyms
problemArchetypes.example: The words 'thrifty,' 'economical,' and 'stingy' all relate to spending little money. Which word has the most negative connotation, and why? Answer: 'stingy,' because it suggests a selfish unwillingness to spend or share, while 'thrifty' and 'economical' suggest a wise and careful use of money.

problemArchetypes.name: Choose the word with the best nuance for the context
problemArchetypes.example: Read the sentence: 'Grandpa never wastes a thing; he reuses every jar and saves every coin, and we admire him for being so ____.' Which word best fits: stingy, thrifty, or cheap? Answer: 'thrifty,' because the sentence shows admiration, and 'thrifty' carries a positive connotation while 'stingy' and 'cheap' are negative.

Easy.description: A single short sentence or line (roughly 8 to 16 words) embedded in the item. The task is identify-level: name the type of figure of speech, state the obvious meaning of a familiar figure, label a clear word relationship (synonym, antonym, part/whole), or pick which of two words is more positive or more negative. Only one concept is tested and the answer is plain from the stimulus.
constraints: Stimulus is one short sentence or line included in the prompt
Tests exactly one concept (one figure of speech, one relationship, or one connotation contrast)
Figures and words are common and familiar to sixth graders (simile, hyperbole, basic personification; synonym/antonym)
Identify-level task: name the figure, state its plain meaning, or pick the more positive or more negative word
No multi-step reasoning; only two answer ideas are in play

Medium.description: A compound or complex sentence or two related sentences (roughly 16 to 35 words) embedded in the item. The task is analyze-level: explain what a personification or metaphor reveals about the thing described, complete a word analogy by naming the relationship, or rank or choose among three near-synonyms by connotation. The student must reason about the relationship or association, not just spot a label.
constraints: Stimulus is a compound or complex sentence, an analogy frame, or a two-sentence pair in the prompt
Tests interpretation of a figure of speech OR a multi-step word relationship (analogy, item/category, cause/effect) OR a three-word connotation scale
Analyze-level task: explain the meaning a figure creates, complete an analogy with justification, or order or select words by nuance
Distractors are plausible partial readings or words with the wrong shade of meaning

Hard.description: A short multi-sentence passage (roughly 3 to 5 sentences, 40 to 75 words) embedded in the item that contains a sustained or subtle figure of speech, or several near-synonyms used together. The task is evaluate-level: judge which interpretation of an extended personification or metaphor best fits the passage, explain how a writer's word choice shapes tone, or select the single near-synonym whose connotation best matches the author's intended attitude. Requires inference about the author's purpose and the surrounding context.
constraints: Stimulus is a 3 to 5 sentence passage included in the prompt
Contains an extended or subtle figure of speech, or a cluster of near-synonyms whose nuances must be weighed against tone
Evaluate-level task: choose the best interpretation or the best-fitting word and justify it from the passage
Requires inference about the author's attitude, tone, or purpose, not just literal meaning

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student reads figurative language literally and reports the surface meaning instead of the intended meaning
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Interprets 'the floorboards groaned and complained' as the boards actually speaking or being alive, rather than as creaking noises described like an unhappy person

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student confuses the labels for figures of speech, mixing up simile, metaphor, personification, and hyperbole
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Labels 'My backpack weighed a thousand pounds' as a simile or personification instead of recognizing it as hyperbole

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student misidentifies the word relationship, treating a part/whole pair as a synonym pair or reversing the direction of an analogy
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Calls 'petal' and 'flower' synonyms, or completes 'finger is to hand as branch is to ____' with 'leaf' or 'wood' instead of 'tree'

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student treats words with the same denotation as fully interchangeable and ignores connotation
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Picks 'stingy' to describe an admired, careful saver because it 'means the same as thrifty,' missing its negative association

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student reverses the connotation scale, judging a negative word as positive or a positive word as negative
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Ranks 'stingy' as more positive than 'thrifty,' or chooses 'cheap' as the praising word in a sentence of admiration

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student ignores tone and context and chooses a near-synonym that clashes with the author's intended attitude
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Fills a sentence of clear admiration with 'cheap' or 'stingy' instead of the context-fitting 'thrifty,' because all three relate to spending little
